title: Three novel Pseudanabaena species (Pseudanabaenales, Cyanobacteriophyta) from frozen glacial and post–glacial lakes in polar regions: Cryotolerance as a potential mechanism for long–term survival of freeze–thaw adapted types
content:
Abstract

Frozen Pseudanabaena-dominated phytobenthic mats were collected from four ecologically similar, shallow, low-conductivity glacial and post-glacial early Holocene lakes in the Arctic and Antarctica. Four isolated strains were subsequently analyzed using a polyphasic approach (morphology, ultrastructure, 16S rRNA gene phylogeny, ITS rRNA region analyses), resulting in the description of three novel Pseudanabaena species (P. gelidogaleata, P. lacugelata, and P. prelichiana). Field observations, complemented with controlled in vitro experiments, confirmed the ability of the new species to withstand freeze–thaw treatments, irrespective of the cryogenic intensity (−20, −80, −196°C). Despite their similar cryoresistance, all species displayed unique phenotypic features—such as cell-shape plasticity with polymorphic “behavior” (within-trichome transitions in morphology), variable constrictions across a range of intensities (including some rare constriction patterns), and different types of swollen/involution cells. These findings, along with ultrastructural observations, blur traditional taxonomic boundaries between Pseudanabaena and related genera. Molecular clock analyses confirmed four diversification lineages within Pseudanabaena and revealed that the three new species represent ancient lineages predating their current habitats, with evolutionary origins dating back to the Mesozoic and Eocene epochs. Overall, the results propose a potential mechanism of long-term survival of Pseudanabaena, probably facilitated by cryopreservation within frozen lakes. Comprehensive molecular analyses strongly suggested a common ancestor between the Arctic P. gelidogaleata and several psychrotolerant strains isolated from Antarctica. This finding may further support the hypothesis of a more global distribution of cold-adapted ecotypes. The study provides new insights into the complex ecology, biogeography, and adaptability of Pseudanabaena cryotypes under extreme conditions.
